title: This popular AI agent could be hacked by a single email — with potentially disastrous consequences
key_facts: Security researchers at Salt Labs found a way around the safety checks of the Manus AI agent using an email, a technique that was later fixed.
The attack only works if the agent is connected to outside services such as email or calendar; a Menlo report says 36% of consumers have given agents access to email.
Manus normally spots a hidden prompt in an email and tells the owner; Salt Labs hid a simple JavaScript command in an unusual disguise called JSFuck.
The agent decoded and ran the command in a server-side environment, so untrusted email content became executable code; Manus warned the owner only after it had run.
Salt Labs disclosed this through Meta's bug bounty program and says it is resolved and no longer exploitable.
Salt Labs' lesson: checks that inspect prompts and model behaviour are necessary but not enough; security must cover what an agent actually does across the tools and systems it can reach.
quote_evidence: Security researchers from Salt Labs have found a way around the guardrails, and while this particular technique was subsequently fixed, chances are there are others out there, just as effective.
Salt Labs said they responsibly disclosed their findings through Meta’s bug bounty program, and that the issue “has since been resolved as is no longer exploitable.”
At this point, we reached a clear security boundary violation: untrusted email content was transformed into executable code and run within the agent’s runtime environment.
why_it_matters_hint: An AI agent connected to email can be tricked into running an attacker's code, even past its own safety checks.
notes: Only a basic test payload was shown, and the flaw is fixed; the article reports no real-world attacks. TechRadar's headline overstates the current risk. Page boilerplate and newsletter text ignored.
